examples.solution_text:
Cut $C$ separates $S$ from $A$, $B$ and $T$. It crosses $SA$ and $SB$, both directed from the source side to the sink side.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Cut capacity} &= 9+4\\&=13\end{aligned}$

Edge $AB$ goes from $A$ on the sink side to $B$ on the source side, so its capacity is not counted. It is neither added nor subtracted.
The forward-crossing edges are $SA$ and $BT$.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Cut capacity} &= 24+23\\&=47\text{ L/s}\end{aligned}$
Line $L$ is not a valid cut. The path $S\to B\to T$ does not cross it, so the line does not completely separate the source from the sink.

Cut $C_1$ crosses $SA$ and $SB$, both forwards.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Capacity of }C_1 &=18+13\\&=31\end{aligned}$
Cut $C_2$ separates $\{S,B\}$ from $\{A,T\}$. Count $SA$ and $BT$; exclude $AB$, which goes from the sink side to the source side.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Capacity of }C_2 &=18+17\\&=35\end{aligned}$
Of these two cuts, $C_1$ has the smaller capacity.

examples.derivation: The vertical cut separates S from A, B and T. Its forward crossings are SA and SB, so its capacity is 9 + 4 = 13.
The diagonal cut places S and B on the source side and A and T on the sink side. SA and BT cross forwards; AB crosses backwards and contributes zero. Capacity = 24 + 23 = 47 L/s.
Line L intersects SA but leaves both SB and BT untouched. The directed path S to B to T remains open, so L is not a valid cut.

C1 separates S from the remaining vertices and has capacity 18 + 13 = 31. C2 separates {S,B} from {A,T}; SA and BT contribute, while AB is excluded. Its capacity is 18 + 17 = 35. Therefore C1 has the smaller capacity of the two.
